blocks.html: C++ was developed by Bjarne Stroustrup at Bell Labs, USA, starting in 1979. It was first called "C with Classes" and renamed C++ in 1983. The name means "one step more than C" (++ is the increment operator).

items.html: Compiled: Programs are converted into fast machine code.
Middle-level: Supports both low-level work (memory, hardware) and high-level work (applications).
Object-oriented: Supports classes and objects (Class 12).
Portable: The same code can be compiled on Windows, Linux and macOS.
Rich library: The Standard Template Library (STL) gives ready-made strings, vectors, maps and algorithms.
Case-sensitive: Total , total and TOTAL are three different names.

blocks.html: Where C++ is used: Operating systems (parts of Windows), browsers (Chrome), games (Unreal Engine), databases (MySQL), banking systems, competitive programming.
Tools you need: A compiler (g++ ) and an editor or IDE such as Code::Blocks, Dev-C++, VS Code, or an online compiler such as OnlineGDB or Programiz.

blocks.html: Character set: Letters (A–Z, a–z), digits (0–9), special symbols (+ - * / % = < > ( ) { } [ ] ; , . ' " # & | ! ? : ~ ^ \ _ ) and white space (space, tab, newline).
A token is the smallest meaningful unit of a program. C++ has five kinds:
(a) Keywords — reserved words with a fixed meaning. They cannot be used as names.

int , float , double , char , bool , void , if , else , switch , case , for , while , do , break , continue , return , const , true , false , struct , class , using , namespace , long , short , unsigned , sizeof , default .
(b) Identifiers — names given to variables, functions, etc.
Rules for identifiers:

items.html: Can contain letters, digits and underscore (_ ) only.
Must begin with a letter or underscore, not a digit.
Cannot be a keyword.
No spaces or special symbols.
Case-sensitive.

blocks.html: (c) Literals (constants) — fixed values written in the program.

items.html: Integer: 25 , -7 , 0x1F (hex), 017 (octal)
Floating point: 3.14 , -0.5 , 2.5e3 (= 2500)
Character: 'A' , '7' , '\n'
String: "Patna" , "Hello World"
Boolean: true , false

blocks.html: (d) Operators — symbols that perform operations (+ , - , == , && , etc.). See 5.7.
(e) Punctuators (separators) — ; , { } ( ) [ ] # : and so on.
A variable is a named memory location that stores a value which can change while the program runs.

blocks.html: (a) Arithmetic operators: + - * / %

items.html: / between two integers gives an integer: 17 / 5 = 3 .
% (modulus) gives the remainder and works only on integers: 17 % 5 = 2 .

blocks.html: (b) Relational operators: < > <= >= == != — give true (1) or false (0).
(c) Logical operators: && (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT)
(d) Assignment operators: = += -= *= /= %= (e.g. x += 5 means x = x + 5 ).
(e) Increment and decrement: ++ and -- .

items.html: Pre-increment ++x : increase first, then use.
Post-increment x++ : use first, then increase.

(a) Implicit conversion (type promotion): Done automatically by the compiler when different types are mixed. The smaller type is converted to the larger type: char → int → long → float → double .

(b) Explicit conversion (type casting): Done by the programmer.

blocks.html: 1. What is a token? Name the types of tokens in C++.
Answer: A token is the smallest meaningful unit of a program. Types: keywords, identifiers, literals, operators and punctuators.
2. Write any four rules for naming identifiers.
Answer: (i) Only letters, digits and underscore are allowed. (ii) Must not start with a digit. (iii) Must not be a keyword. (iv) No spaces; names are case-sensitive.
3. Differentiate between x++ and ++x with an example.
Answer: x++ (post-increment) uses the value first and then increases it; ++x (pre- increment) increases first and then uses it. With x = 5 : y = x++ gives y = 5, x = 6; y = ++x gives y = 6, x = 6.
4. What is the difference between = and == ?
Answer: = is the assignment operator; it stores a value (a = 5 ). == is the relational equality operator; it compares two values and gives true or false (a == 5 ).
5. What is type casting? Give an example.
Answer: Type casting is converting a value from one data type to another by the programmer. Example: float avg = (float)total / 5; converts total to float so that decimal division happens.
6. Write the output:

blocks.code:
int x = 10, y = 3;
cout << x / y * y + x % y;

blocks.html: Answer: 10 . x / y = 3; 3 × 3 = 9; x % y = 1; 9 + 1 = 10.
7. Why is using namespace std; written in a C++ program?
Answer: The names cout , cin , endl and string belong to the standard namespace
std . This line lets us use them directly instead of writing std::cout every time.
8. Differentiate between a syntax error and a logical error.

Answer: A syntax error breaks the language rules and is caught by the compiler (e.g. missing ; ). A logical error is a mistake in the program's logic; it compiles and runs but gives a wrong answer (e.g. avg = a + b / 2 ).
9. Rewrite using the ternary operator:

blocks.code: if (marks >= 33) result = "Pass"; else result = "Fail";

blocks.html: Answer: result = (marks >= 33) ? "Pass" : "Fail";
10. Find the output: int p = 4; p += p * 2; cout << p;
Answer: 12 . p += 8 means p = 4 + 8 = 12.
1. Explain the structure of a C++ program with an example.

Answer: See section 5.2. A C++ program has: comments (documentation), preprocessor directives (#include <iostream> ), the namespace declaration (using namespace std; ), the main() function where execution begins, statements inside braces each ending with ; , and return 0; to end successfully.
2. Explain the basic data types of C++ with their sizes and examples.

Answer: See the table in 5.4: int (4 bytes, whole numbers), float (4 bytes, ~7 digit decimals), double (8 bytes, ~15 digit decimals), char (1 byte, one character), bool (1 byte, true/false), string (text), void (no value). Modifiers like long long and
unsigned change range.
